ex.he: מספר הטלפון שלי מתחיל באפס חמש.
ex.en: My phone number starts with zero five.

note: Same for both genders. Phone numbers are usually read digit by digit with the counting forms, and Israeli mobile numbers start with 05: אפס חמש…

ex.en: It's one o'clock now.

note: Hebrew numbers come in two sets. This is the feminine form, which is also used for counting, clock times and phone numbers. Masculine: אחד (ekhád). Unlike the other numbers, one comes after the noun: בת אחת (one daughter), ילד אחד (one boy).

ex.en: How many cups of coffee? Two, please.

note: Feminine/counting form; masculine שניים (shnáyim). Before a noun both get shorter: שתי בנות (shtei banót, two girls), שני ילדים (shnei yeladím, two boys). Time words often use a dual ending instead: שעתיים (two hours), יומיים (two days).

ex.en: I have three sisters.

note: Feminine/counting form, used with feminine nouns: שלוש אחיות. Masculine: שלושה (shloshá), used with masculine nouns: שלושה אחים (three brothers). Surprise: from 3 to 10 it is the masculine form that ends in ־ה.

ex.en: My daughter is four.

note: Masculine: ארבעה (arba'á): ארבעה ימים (four days). Ages always use the counting form, for boys too: הוא בן ארבע, היא בת ארבע.

ex.en: Samir finishes work at five.

note: Masculine: חמישה (khamishá): חמישה שקלים (five shekels). Clock times use the counting form: בחמש = at five.

ex.en: Tamar gets up at six in the morning.

note: Masculine: שישה (shishá): שישה חודשים (six months).

ex.en: The shop is open until seven.

note: Masculine: שבעה (shiv'á): שבעה ימים (seven days). שבוע (week) comes from the same root.

ex.en: They work eight hours a day.

note: The feminine shmoné (in everyday speech usually shmóne) and the masculine shmoná are spelled the same: שמונה שעות (f), שמונה ימים (m).

ex.en: The film starts at nine.

note: Masculine: תשעה (tish'á): תשעה חודשים (nine months).

ex.en: Anna needs ten more minutes.

note: Masculine: עשרה (asará): עשרה שקלים (ten shekels). Don't mix it up with ־עשרה (esré), the ending of the feminine numbers 11–19: אחת עשרה.

ex.en: It's already eleven at night.

note: Feminine/counting form: in 11–19 the feminine numbers add עשרה (esré). Masculine: אחד עשר (akhad asár): אחד עשר שחקנים (eleven players).

ex.en: We have lunch at twelve.

note: Masculine: שנים עשר (shnem asár): שנים עשר חודשים (twelve months). Note the short forms שתים / שנים here, not שתיים / שניים.

ex.he: בכיתה יש שלוש עשרה בנות ושנים עשר בנים.
ex.en: There are thirteen girls and twelve boys in the class.

note: Masculine: שלושה עשר (shlosha asár). The pattern of 3–10 continues in 13–19: the feminine uses the short form (שלוש), the masculine the form with ־ה (שלושה).

ex.en: My son is fourteen.

note: Masculine: ארבעה עשר (arba'a asár). Ages use the feminine form even for boys, because the unspoken word שנים (years) is feminine: בן ארבע עשרה.

ex.he: יש הפסקה של חמש עשרה דקות.
ex.en: There's a fifteen-minute break.

note: Masculine: חמישה עשר (khamisha asár). In speech, fifteen minutes is usually רבע שעה (a quarter of an hour).

ex.he: בבניין שלנו יש שש עשרה דירות.
ex.en: There are sixteen apartments in our building.

note: Masculine: שישה עשר (shisha asár).

ex.en: Our office is on the seventeenth floor.

note: Masculine: שבעה עשר (shiv'a asár). The vowels change: on its own it's shéva, in 17 it's shva. Floors, rooms and bus lines put the plain number after the noun: קומה שבע עשרה.

ex.en: There are eighteen questions on the exam.

note: Masculine: שמונה עשר (shmona asár). In Jewish tradition 18 stands for חי (life), so gifts of money often come in multiples of 18, such as 180 or 360 shekels.

ex.he: אני נוסעת לעבודה בקו תשע עשרה.
ex.en: I take bus number nineteen to work.

note: Masculine: תשעה עשר (tish'a asár). The vowels change, as in 17: on its own it's tésha, in 19 it's tsha. Bus lines are read in the counting form: קו תשע עשרה = bus number 19.

ex.en: The falafel costs twenty shekels.

note: The tens are the same for both genders. 21 = עשרים ואחת (f) / עשרים ואחד (m). After numbers above ten, some common nouns usually stay singular: עשרים שקל, עשרים שנה, עשרים יום.

ex.en: September has thirty days.

note: Built on שלוש + ־ים, like most of the tens. The same for both genders: שלושים ילדים, שלושים ילדות.

ex.en: The ride to work takes forty minutes.

note: Compound numbers join the last part with ו: ארבעים וחמש (45).

ex.en: I only have fifty shekels.

note: A fifty-shekel note is שטר של חמישים. The same for both genders.

ex.en: There are sixty minutes in an hour.

note: Built on שש (six): שש → שישים, just as שלוש → שלושים.

ex.en: Adisu's grandmother is seventy.

note: Built on שבע, but with the vowels of the masculine שבעה (shiv'á).

ex.en: This shirt costs eighty shekels.

note: Built on שמונה + ־ים. The same for both genders.

ex.he: יש לנו דירה של תשעים מטר.
ex.en: We have a ninety-square-meter apartment.

note: Apartment sizes are given in square meters, usually just called מטר: דירה של תשעים מטר.

ex.en: The meal costs a hundred shekels per person.

note: מאה is feminine, so the hundreds use the feminine numbers: מאתיים (200), שלוש מאות (300), תשע מאות (900). Plural מאות (me'ót).

ex.en: The new bike costs a thousand shekels.

note: אלף is masculine: אלפיים (2,000), then the short masculine forms: שלושת אלפים (3,000), עשרת אלפים (10,000). Plural אלפים (alafím).

ex.en: What's your phone number?

note: A single digit is ספרה. In a shoe shop, מה המספר שלך? = what size are you? In formal Hebrew מספר also means 'several': מספר אנשים.

ex.en: It's my first day at work.

note: Feminine ראשונה (rishoná). יום ראשון = Sunday, the first working day of the Israeli week. Same root as ראש (head).

ex.he: הבן השני של מרינה בן שש.
ex.en: Marina's second son is six.

note: Feminine שנייה (shniyá), which also means 'a second' of time: שנייה! / רק שנייה! = just a sec! יום שני = Monday. Don't confuse it with שני (shnei), the form of 'two' before a masculine noun: שני ילדים.

ex.en: This is Nour's third book.

note: Feminine שלישית (shlishít). יום שלישי = Tuesday. Most ordinals add ־י to the number: שלוש → שלישי.

ex.en: Our house is the fourth on the street.

note: Feminine רביעית (revi'ít). יום רביעי = Wednesday. Same root as רבע (a quarter).

ex.en: This is our fifth lesson.

note: Feminine חמישית (khamishít). יום חמישי = Thursday, the last day of the working week in most Israeli offices.

ex.en: This is my sixth coffee today!

note: Feminine שישית (shishít). יום שישי = Friday; שישי-שבת or סוף שבוע (סופ״ש) = the weekend.

ex.en: Shabbat is the seventh day of the week.

note: Feminine שביעית (shvi'ít). Saturday is simply called שבת, not יום שביעי.

ex.en: This is my eighth month in Israel.

note: Feminine שמינית (shminít). בארץ (lit. 'in the land') is how Israelis usually say 'in Israel'.

ex.en: September is the ninth month of the year.

note: Feminine תשיעית (tshi'ít).

ex.he: היום יום ההולדת העשירי של נועם.
ex.en: Today is Noam's tenth birthday.

note: Feminine עשירית (asirít), also 'a tenth' (0.1). Not to be confused with עשיר (ashír, rich). From 11 up there are no special ordinals, just the number: הקומה ה-11 (the 11th floor).

ex.en: I'll be there in half an hour.

note: Before a noun: חצי שעה, חצי עוגה. After a number it becomes וחצי: שעתיים וחצי (two and a half hours), שלוש וחצי (half past three).

ex.en: It's a quarter past three.

note: Telling the time: שלוש ורבע = 3:15, רבע לארבע = 3:45 (a quarter to four). רבע שעה = fifteen minutes.

ex.en: I need a pair of socks.

note: Masculine, but the plural ends in ־ות: זוגות. Also 'a couple': הם זוג (they're a couple). Things that come in pairs often have a dual ending: נעליים, גרביים.

ex.en: I have a lot of work today.

note: Comes before the noun and never changes: הרבה אנשים, הרבה מים. After a verb: אני עובד הרבה (I work a lot). 'Thanks a lot' is תודה רבה, not הרבה.

ex.en: John speaks a little Hebrew.

note: Before nouns and adjectives: קצת מים, קצת עייף (a bit tired). עוד קצת = a little more.

ex.en: Today is hotter than yesterday.

note: Comparatives: יותר גדול or גדול יותר (bigger). יותר מ = more than: יותר ממאה שקל. יותר מדי = too much.

ex.en: There are fewer people on the bus today.

note: פחות או יותר = more or less. In arithmetic it means minus: עשר פחות שלוש זה שבע (ten minus three is seven).

ex.en: Which color do you like, Yael?

note: Colors are adjectives and agree with the noun: חולצה כחולה, מכנסיים כחולים. צבע also means paint.

ex.en: My red bag is on the table.

note: Feminine אדומה (adumá); plural אדומים, אדומות. In most colors the o turns into u before an ending: adóm → adumá.

ex.en: The sea is blue and beautiful today.

note: Feminine כחולה (kkhulá); plural כחולים, כחולות. Light blue is תכלת.

ex.en: The light is green, you can cross.

note: Feminine ירוקה (yeruká); plural ירוקים, ירוקות. Same root as ירקות (vegetables).

ex.en: He has a yellow hat.

note: Feminine צהובה (tsehubá); plural צהובים, צהובות.

ex.en: I'd like white wine, please.

note: Feminine לבנה (levaná); plural לבנים, לבנות. The soft white cheese (labneh) is also written לבנה.

ex.he: אני שותה קפה שחור בלי סוכר.
ex.en: I drink black coffee without sugar.

note: Feminine שחורה (shkhorá); plural שחורים, שחורות. In Israel קפה שחור usually means Turkish-style coffee, also called קפה בוץ ('mud coffee').

ex.en: We have a brown dog.

note: Feminine חומה (khumá); plural חומים, חומות. Spelled like the noun חום (khom, heat; fever).

ex.en: It's a gray, cold day.

note: Feminine אפורה (afurá); plural אפורים, אפורות. Same root as אפר (ash).

ex.en: My daughter only likes pink.

note: Feminine ורודה (vrudá); plural ורודים, ורודות. Same root as ורד (rose).

ex.en: I like the color orange.

note: Feminine כתומה (ktumá); plural כתומים, כתומות. The fruit is תפוז.

ex.en: Your purple sweater is pretty.

note: Feminine סגולה (sgulá); plural סגולים, סגולות.

ex.en: I have a light-blue shirt.

note: Originally a noun, so it never changes: חולצה תכלת, מכנסיים תכלת.

ex.en: We have a big kitchen.

note: Feminine גדולה (gdolá); plural גדולים, גדולות. Bigger = יותר גדול. Slang: אתה גדול! = you're great!

ex.en: My room is small but comfortable.

note: Feminine קטנה (ktaná); plural קטנים, קטנות. הקטן / הקטנה = the youngest child in the family.

ex.en: It's a very long day.

note: Feminine ארוכה (arukhá), which sounds exactly like ארוחה (meal). Plural ארוכים, ארוכות.

ex.en: The film is short, only an hour.

note: Feminine קצרה (ktsará); plural קצרים, קצרות. For things and time; a short person is נמוך.

ex.en: Omer is very tall.

note: Feminine גבוהה (gvohá); plural גבוהים, גבוהות. Also 'high': מחיר גבוה (a high price).

ex.en: This table is too low.

note: Feminine נמוכה (nemukhá); plural נמוכים, נמוכות. Short people are נמוכים, short things are קצרים.

ex.en: This street is wide and quiet.

note: Feminine רחבה (rekhavá); plural רחבים, רחבות. Same root as רחוב (street).

ex.en: The room is narrow and long.

note: Feminine צרה (tsará), which also means 'trouble'; plural צרים, צרות. For clothes it means tight. צר לי = I'm sorry.

ex.en: We have a round table in the kitchen.

note: Feminine עגולה (agulá); plural עגולים, עגולות. מספר עגול = a round number.

ex.en: This book is very heavy.

note: Feminine כבדה (kvedá); plural כבדים, כבדות. The noun כבד, said the same way, means liver.

ex.en: That's a good idea!

note: Feminine טובה (tová); plural טובים, טובות. On its own it means 'OK, well': טוב, נתראה מחר. בוקר טוב = good morning.

ex.en: That's not bad at all!

note: Feminine רעה (ra'á); plural רעים, רעות. רע לי = I feel bad, I'm unhappy. In everyday speech לא טוב is often used instead of רע.

ex.en: I have a new phone.

note: Feminine חדשה (khadashá); plural חדשים, חדשות. חדשות also means 'the news'. מה חדש? = what's new?

ex.en: Our building is old but beautiful.

note: Feminine ישנה (yeshaná); plural ישנים, ישנות. For things only; an old person is מבוגר or זקן. Spelled like ישן (yashén, sleeping).

ex.en: The new doctor is very young.

note: Feminine צעירה (tse'irá); plural צעירים, צעירות. צעירים on its own also means 'young people'.

ex.en: Our dog is already old.

note: Feminine זקנה (zkená); plural זקנים, זקנות. For people and animals; about people, מבוגר (older) is more polite. The noun זקן (zakán) means beard.

ex.en: The tea is still too hot.

note: Feminine חמה (khamá); plural חמים, חמות. חם לי = I'm hot (lit. 'it's hot to me'); חם היום = it's hot today.

ex.en: I'm cold, where's my coat?

note: Feminine קרה (kará); plural קרים, קרות. קר לי = I'm cold; מים קרים = cold water.

ex.en: This is an easy exercise.

note: Feminine קלה (kalá); plural קלים, קלות. Also 'light' (not heavy): תיק קל. בקלות = easily.

ex.he: עברית היא שפה קשה, אבל יפה.
ex.en: Hebrew is a hard language, but a beautiful one.

note: The feminine is spelled the same, קשה, but said kashá. Also 'hard' (not soft): לחם קשה. קשה לי = it's hard for me.

ex.en: The coffee here is cheap and good.

note: Feminine זולה (zolá); plural זולים, זולות. The opposite is יקר (expensive). זול יותר = cheaper.

ex.en: What a beautiful day today!

note: The feminine is spelled the same, יפה, but said yafá. Plural יפים, יפות. יפה! on its own = well done! / nice!

ex.en: The kitchen is clean now.

note: Feminine נקייה (nekiyá); plural נקיים, נקיות. Same root as לנקות (to clean) and ניקיון (cleaning).

ex.en: The table is dirty, it needs cleaning.

note: Feminine מלוכלכת (melukhlékhet); plural מלוכלכים, מלוכלכות. לכלוך = dirt.

ex.en: The bus is full, there's no room.

note: Feminine מלאה (mle'á); plural מלאים, מלאות. מלא ב = full of. Colloquially מלא also means 'lots of': יש לי מלא עבודה.

ex.en: The fridge is empty, we need to buy food.

note: Feminine ריקה (reká); plural ריקים, ריקות. על בטן ריקה = on an empty stomach.

ex.en: The internet here is very fast.

note: Feminine מהירה (mehirá); plural מהירים, מהירות (also the noun 'speed'). The adverb is מהר (mahér, quickly): בוא מהר!

ex.en: My computer is slow today.

note: Feminine איטית (itít); plural איטיים, איטיות. The adverb is לאט (le'át, slowly); לאט לאט = little by little.

ex.en: I'm happy to see you!

note: Feminine שמחה (smekhá); plural שמחים, שמחות. חג שמח! = happy holiday! The noun שמחה (simkhá) = joy; a celebration.

ex.en: Why are you sad today, Igor?

note: Feminine עצובה (atsuvá); plural עצובים, עצובות. עצוב לי = I feel sad.

ex.en: I'm tired, I'm going to bed.

note: Feminine עייפה (ayefá); plural עייפים, עייפות. Very common: אני מת מעייפות (I'm dead tired, lit. 'dying of tiredness').

ex.en: I'm hungry, what is there to eat?

note: Feminine רעבה (re'evá); plural רעבים, רעבות. אני מת מרעב = I'm starving. The noun רעב (ra'áv) = hunger.

ex.en: The boy is thirsty; is there any water here?

note: Feminine צמאה (tsme'á); plural צמאים, צמאות. אני מת מצמא = I'm dying of thirst.
